steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Reconstructing high-quality surface normals is very important in computer vision and graphics, for 3D reconstruction, relighting, and inverse rendering. Among the different techniques, photometric stereo uses the variation of intensity of a scene point under different illumination conditions to reconstruct normals. Photometric stereo is used in various imaging systems, including light stages, handheld-flash cameras, and display-camera systems.

Display photometric stereo uses monitors and cameras, which is a versatile and accessible system that can be placed on a desk easily. Diverse illumination conditions can be produced simply by displaying multiple patterns, with the pixels on the display used as programmable point light sources. Because the illumination conditions can be modulated so conveniently and intricately, the design space of illumination patterns for display photometric stereo becomes much larger. But existing approaches often use heuristic display patterns, and this gives sub-optimal reconstruction quality.

  - 3D-printed training dataset with known geometry -> normal loss; efficient, realistic relit image simulation
  - LCD emits polarized light -> polarization camera removes specular reflection

  - learned patterns >> heuristic ones on diverse objects

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Reconstructing high-quality surface normals is very important in computer vision and graphics, for 3D reconstruction, relighting, and inverse rendering. Among the different techniques, photometric stereo uses the variation of intensity of a scene point under different illumination conditions to reconstruct normals. Photometric stereo is used in various imaging systems, including light stages, handheld-flash cameras, and display-camera systems.

Display photometric stereo uses monitors and cameras, which is a versatile and accessible system that can be placed on a desk easily. Diverse illumination conditions can be produced simply by displaying multiple patterns, with the pixels on the display used as programmable point light sources. Because the illumination conditions can be modulated so conveniently and intricately, the design space of illumination patterns for display photometric stereo becomes much larger. But existing approaches often use heuristic display patterns, and this gives sub-optimal reconstruction quality.

In this paper we propose differentiable display photometric stereo (DDPS), to exploit the large design space of illumination patterns in display photometric stereo. The key idea is to learn, end-to-end, display patterns that give better reconstruction of surface normals for a target system. For this we introduce a differentiable framework that combines basis-illumination image formation with an optimization-based photometric stereo method. This makes pattern learning effective, since the display patterns are directly optimized with auto-differentiation. To compute the normal-reconstruction loss for backpropagation, we propose to use 3D printing to create a real-world training dataset where the geometry is known. Together with the basis-illumination image formation, the 3D-printed dataset lets us simulate relit images efficiently and realistically during end-to-end optimization. We also use the fact that conventional LCD monitors emit polarized light. So with a polarization camera we can optically remove specular reflection, which often makes photometric-stereo reconstruction worse.

We evaluate DDPS extensively on diverse objects, and using the learned patterns improves normal accuracy significantly compared to using heuristic patterns. DDPS is also robust to pattern initialization, calibration error, and simplifications in image formation and reconstruction, so it promises to be practically applicable. We will release code and data upon acceptance.

Our contributions are:

- Instead of using heuristic patterns for display photometric stereo, we directly learn display patterns end-to-end that lead to high-quality normal reconstruction for display photometric stereo.

- For DDPS we propose a differentiable framework with basis-illumination image formation and analytic photometric-stereo reconstruction, the use of 3D-printed objects for a training dataset, and the use of a polarized LCD and a polarization camera.

- We do extensive experiments that show the effectiveness of the learned patterns, which outperform heuristic patterns, and the robustness of DDPS against various factors, including pattern initialization and calibration errors.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Reconstructing high-quality surface normals is pivotal in computer vision and graphics for 3D reconstruction [1], relighting [2,3], and inverse rendering [4,5]. Among the various techniques, photometric stereo [6] leverages the intensity variation of a scene point under varied illumination conditions to reconstruct normals. Photometric stereo is applied in various imaging systems, including light stages [7,8,9], handheld-flash cameras [10,5,11,12], and display-camera systems [13,14].

Display photometric stereo uses monitors and cameras as a versatile and accessible system that can be conveniently placed on a desk [13,14]. Diverse illumination conditions can be produced simply by displaying multiple patterns, using the pixels of the display as programmable point light sources. This convenient and intricate modulation of illumination conditions significantly enlarges the design space of illumination patterns for display photometric stereo. However, existing approaches often rely on heuristic display patterns, which results in sub-optimal reconstruction quality.

In this paper, we propose differentiable display photometric stereo (DDPS) to exploit the large design space of illumination patterns in display photometric stereo. The key idea is to learn, in an end-to-end manner, display patterns that lead to improved surface-normal reconstruction for a target system. To this end, we introduce a differentiable framework that combines basis-illumination image formation with an optimization-based photometric stereo method. This enables effective pattern learning by directly optimizing the display patterns via auto-differentiation. To compute the normal-reconstruction loss for backpropagation, we propose using 3D printing to create a real-world training dataset with known geometry. Combined with the basis-illumination image formation, the 3D-printed dataset allows efficient and realistic simulation of relit images during end-to-end optimization. In addition, we leverage the fact that conventional LCD monitors emit polarized light: using a polarization camera, we can optically remove specular reflection, which often deteriorates photometric-stereo reconstruction.

Extensive evaluation of DDPS on diverse objects shows that the learned patterns significantly improve normal accuracy compared to heuristic patterns. Moreover, DDPS is robust to pattern initialization, calibration error, and simplifications in image formation and reconstruction, which promises practical applicability. We will release code and data upon acceptance.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- • Departing from heuristic patterns for display photometric stereo, we directly learn display patterns that lead to high-quality normal reconstruction in an end-to-end manner.

- • For DDPS, we propose a differentiable framework consisting of basis-illumination image formation and analytic photometric-stereo reconstruction, the use of 3D-printed objects as a training dataset, and the use of a polarized LCD and a polarization camera.

- • We perform extensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the learned patterns, which outperform heuristic patterns, and the robustness of DDPS against various factors, including pattern initialization and calibration errors.
